passage: Sumit, you asked why I still call my mother every Sunday, though she once made me feel like a traitor for leaving. Sit; I will tell you. At twenty-four I got an offer from a firm two cities away. My mother stopped speaking to me for nine days, and I lay awake feeling like a traitor. Then came the headaches every time I mentioned it, and the line, "Go, go, if it finishes me, so be it." I nearly turned the offer down. What changed was a cousin saying, "Love could have said I will miss you." So I told my mother, gently, that I was going, that I would call every Sunday and come home for every festival. She sulked for a month, then began posting me pickles. The guilt lasted longer than the sulk. Mridul

qa.q: How many days did Mridul's mother stop speaking after the offer?
qa.a: She stopped speaking to Mridul for nine days.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling during the nine days of silence?
qa.a: Mridul felt guilty and torn, lying awake feeling like a traitor.

qa.q: How did Mridul set a boundary while keeping warmth?
qa.a: Mridul said gently that the move was happening and promised to call every Sunday and come home for every festival.

qa.q: How might the mother have seen the move?
qa.a: Her silence and talk of being finished suggest she feared being left alone, though it was not a fair way to say so.

grounding: An elder recalls a parent controlling through silence, headaches and guilt, and how gentle firm boundaries and warmth carried through.
